newsitem.title: India: India hopeful after Sharif's win in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: India hopeful after Sharif's win in Pakistan.

text.p: India said on Tuesday it was hopeful of better ties with arch-rival Pakistan under a new government led by Nawaz Sharif, but analysts cautioned they did not foresee a radical change in Islamabad's foreign policy.

India's Foreign Ministry said it hoped the new Pakistan government would respond to an offer made by Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda shortly after he took office last June to restart talks between senior officials.
"Let the new Pakistan government be sworn in and we will wait for a response," Foreign Ministry spokesman Talmiz Ahmed told a news conference.

"India has sent a letter to the Pakistani government for bilateral talks and we hope the new government will respond to it positively," the Press Trust of India quoted Defence Minister Malayam Singh Yadav as saying in the northern city of Lucknow.
The Pakistan Muslim League (PML) led by former prime minister Nawaz Sharif scored a resounding victory over Benazir Bhutto in Monday's national election.
Pakistan President Farooq Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government last November accusing it of corruption and misrule.
"This is also the first time that a leader of Mr Sharif's stature has not taken an anti-India stand during the election campaign," Yadav was quoted as saying.

India was interested in holding an official dialogue with Pakistan on all issues, Ahmed said. "We have had no response so far. We hope the new government will give a response...We would welcome a resumption of the dialogue between two countries if Pakistan wants it."
The latest results showed Sharif's party had secured 128 seats of the 189 results declared in the 217-member National Assembly while Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party was straggling in with 17 seats.

"There is hope that normal dialogues will be revived under Nawaz Sharif not immediately but over a six-month period," Brahma Chellaney, an analyst with Centre for Policy Research, a private think-tank, told Reuters.
Carved out of British India in 1947 in a bloodstained partition of the subcontinent, India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over the troubled Kashmir region.
The neighbours have not held official talks for more than three years, mainly because of deep differences over Kashmir.
Analysts noted that Sharif, during his earlier prime ministership between 1990 to 1993, had held several meetings with then Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.

"During his election campaign Sharif made suggestions to improve bilateral relations through dialogue," said J.N. Dixit, a former foreign secretary. "We should be responsive to suggestions made by Sharif on normalisation of relations."
But Chellaney said so far as broad foreign policy was concerned there were unlikely to be major changes.
"Not many changes in the overall foreign policy are foreseen," he said. "The main question is to clean up the (Pakistan) economic situation."
